checks.do: Whether peak CPU and memory stay under the group-wide thresholds with one App Connector of the group unavailable, and whether a CPU figure above 100% is normalized by the core count.
Whether a high CPU steal percentage in the local status log points to the hypervisor rather than the App Connector.
Whether the in-use TCP or UDP port count is equal or close to the available ports on the host.
Whether any App Connector approaches 6,000 application targets, at which On Access health reporting becomes None.

surfaces.statement: Within the Admin Console the App Connector Dashboard and Health Dashboard help monitor an organization's App Connectors; the page's most important point is that App Connectors are deployed following Zscaler's recommendations for image sizing and scalability, supported platform requirements, deployment best practices, networking configurations and other essential guidelines.

quotes: Within the Zscaler Admin Console, you can use the App Connector Dashboard and Health Dashboard to help you monitor your organization's App Connectors.

The most important thing is to make sure your App Connectors are deployed in a manner that follows Zscaler's recommendations for image sizing and scalability, supported platform requirements, deployment best practices, networking configurations, and other essential guidelines.

cpu-headroom.statement: Peak CPU utilization should be less than 75%, taking into account all connectors in the group, so that each App Connector can operate under 75% utilization if one of the group's App Connectors becomes unavailable; in the page's example, two App Connectors both at 50% are below the 75% threshold, but if one goes down the other runs above 75%.

quotes: Peak CPU utilization should be less than 75%. The value needs to take into account all connectors in the group.

The CPU utilization of the group's App Connectors should be able to manage additional load and allow each App Connector to operate under 75% utilization in the event one of the App Connectors becomes unavailable.
For example, if you only have two App Connectors and they are both at 50%, this is below the 75% threshold. However, if one App Connector goes down, then the other App Connector is running above 75%.

memory-headroom.statement: Peak memory utilization should be less than 90%, and the memory of the group's App Connectors should allow each App Connector to operate under 90% utilization if one of them becomes unavailable.

quotes: Peak memory utilization should be less than 90%.

The memory of the group's App Connectors should be able to manage additional load and allow each App Connector to operate under 90% utilization in the event one of the App Connectors becomes unavailable.

throughput-ceiling.statement: Peak throughput based on recommended App Connector specifications should be less than 500 Mbps, and the 500 Mbps is an aggregate of multiple streams of traffic.

quotes: Peak throughput based on recommended App Connector specifications should be less than 500 Mbps.
500 Mbps of throughput is an aggregate of multiple streams of traffic.

lss-status-fields.statement: App Connector Status logs can be streamed to a SIEM or syslog server using the Log Streaming Service (LSS) and are generated periodically for each connector; the field CPUUtilization displays the App Connector host's CPU utilization at that instance, MemUtilization its memory utilization and TotalBytesRx and TotalBytesTx its throughput.

quotes: App Connector Status logs can be streamed to a SIEM or a syslog server using the Log Streaming Service (LSS).
App Connector Status logs are generated periodically for each connector, and the field CPUUtilization displays the App Connector host’s CPU utilization at that instance.
App Connector Status logs are generated periodically for each connector, and the field MemUtilization displays the App Connector host’s memory utilization at that instance.
App Connector Status logs are generated periodically for each connector, and the fields TotalBytesRx and TotalBytesTx display the App Connector host’s throughput at that instance.

cpu-steal.statement: App Connector logs can be viewed on the App Connector host whenever the App Connector is running; CPU steal percentage, the CPU time stolen from the VM by a hypervisor, is reported every minute in the status log. When it is high the hypervisor is busy, resulting in degraded performance for the App Connector, and the page says to ensure the hypervisor is healthy and change the hypervisor setup accordingly.

quotes: App Connector logs can be viewed on the App Connector host whenever the App Connector is running.
CPU steal percentage is the CPU time stolen from the VM by a Hypervisor and is reported every minute in the status log.
When the CPU steal percentage is high, the Hypervisor is busy, resulting in degraded performance for the App Connector.
Ensure the Hypervisor is healthy.
Change the Hypervisor setup accordingly.

cpu-normalize-cores.statement: The top command reports the sum of utilization across all cores on all processors, so a CPU utilization above 100% might be due to multiple CPU cores on the App Connector host (for example, 4 cores could show usage at 400%); the lscpu command shows the number of CPU cores, and the calculation of peak CPU should be normalized across the number of cores.

quotes: The top command reports the sum of utilization across all cores on all processors.
If the CPU utilization is more than 100%, it might be due to multiple CPU cores on the App Connector host. For example, if there are 4 cores, the top output could show usage at 400%.
Use the lscpu command to check the number of CPU cores. In this case, the calculation of peak CPU should be normalized across the number of cores.

scale-out-remedies.statement: Under each of the CPU, memory and data throughput headings the page recommends deploying additional App Connectors into the App Connector group to distribute users across additional connectors, and deploying dedicated App Connector groups for specific application segments to reduce the number of applications requested through each App Connector group; for memory it also recommends increasing the amount of available memory on the App Connector host.

evidence.after: To reduce the CPU utilization on individual App Connector hosts, consider the following:
quotes: Deploy additional App Connectors into the App Connector group to distribute users across additional connectors.
Deploy dedicated App Connector groups for specific application segments to reduce the number of applications that are requested through each App Connector group.

evidence.after: To reduce memory utilization on individual App Connector hosts, consider the following:
quotes: Deploy additional App Connectors into the App Connector group to distribute users across additional connectors.
Deploy dedicated App Connector groups for specific application segments to reduce the number of applications that are requested through each App Connector group.
Increase the amount of available memory on the App Connector host.

evidence.after: To reduce data throughput on individual App Connector hosts, consider the following:
quotes: Deploy additional App Connectors into the App Connector group to distribute users across additional connectors.
Deploy dedicated App Connector groups for specific application segments to reduce the number of applications that are requested through each App Connector group.

source-port-exhaustion.statement: If the in-use count for either TCP or UDP ports is equal or close to the available ports, the App Connector host is likely to experience port exhaustion and the App Connector might not be able to connect to the application servers; in the page's example the difference 60999-32768=28231 is the number of ports available on that host. The page's remedies are to increase the available maximum number of ports (a non-permanent increase does not persist across the App Connector host restart; a permanent one is added to /etc/sysctl.conf), assign a secondary IP address to the existing interface, or create an additional interface; the page says the secondary address and the additional interface each give the host an additional set of TCP ports.

quotes: If the in-use count for either TCP or UDP ports is equal or close to the available ports, the App Connector host is likely to experience port exhaustion and the App Connector might not be able to connect to the application servers.
It shows the difference of 60999-32768=28231, which indicates the number of ports available for use on this App Connector host.
Increase the available max number of ports.
For a non-permanent increase in ports, which does not persist across the App Connector host restart, use one of the following options.
For a permanent increase in ports, add the following to /etc/sysctl.conf.
Assign a secondary IP address to the existing interface.
The number of TCP ports available to the App Connector host can be increased by adding another IP address to the existing interface.
This allows the host to access applications using the secondary IP address in combination with an additional set of TCP ports.
Create an additional interface on the App Connector host. The additional interface enables the host to use an additional set of TCP ports when accessing applications through this interface.

source-port-exhaustion.conditions: The 32768 to 60999 range is the example host's, not a stated default.

application-target-limit.statement: Starting with App Connector version 20.11.20, each App Connector records the number of applications it is currently monitoring for reachability. An App Connector can monitor at most 6,000 application targets at any time, so application definitions must be distributed across multiple application segments and App Connector groups to keep each connector under 6,000; if an App Connector reaches 6,000 targets, the On Access health reporting of the application is converted to None, which means the App Connector does not check and report reachability to the application.

quotes: Starting with App Connector version 20.11.20, each App Connector records the number of applications that it is currently monitoring for reachability.
An App Connector can only monitor a maximum of 6,000 application targets at any given time.

Customers must distribute their application definitions across multiple Application Segments and App Connector groups to ensure that the maximum application targets monitored by an App Connector are less than 6,000.

In the case that an App Connector reaches the maximum 6,000 application targets, the On Access health reporting of your application is converted to None, which means that the App Connector does not check and report reachability to the application.

target-count-field-name.statement: The monitoring page says the monitored-application count is stored in the current_target_count field of the App Connector status logs.

quotes: Starting with App Connector version 20.11.20, each App Connector records the number of applications that it is currently monitoring for reachability.
This value is stored in the current_target_count field of the App Connector status logs.

target-count-on-host.statement: On the host, the page's example greps the journal for target (journalctl -n1000 | grep target) and shows a line with registered apps count 1, alive apps 1, apps with on-access health 1, service count 0, target count 3466 and target alive 3466.

quotes: journalctl -n1000 | grep target
Registered apps count 1, alive apps 1, apps with on-access health 1, service count 0, target count 3466, target alive 3466

target-count-on-host.conditions: Example output only; the page's values illustrate the line's shape.

disk-restart.statement: The App Connector process restarts if there is less than 100 MB of disk space left, and generates a log in /var/log/message to reflect the cause, so that software updates for the App Connector can download successfully. If the App Connector runs other software it can generate large volumes of logs that fill the disk; Zscaler recommends at least disabling rsyslogd to reduce disk space, and the page's example is that deleting /var/log/messages has no functional implication.

quotes: The App Connector process restarts if there is less than 100 MB of disk space left, and it generates a log in /var/log/message file to reflect the cause of the restart. This is done to ensure software updates for the App Connector can download successfully.
If the App Connector runs other software, it can generate large volumes of logs that can fill up the disk space.
Zscaler recommends at least disabling rsyslogd to reduce disk space.
For example, there is no functional implication for deleting /var/log/messages.

file-descriptors.statement: If the number of file descriptors is not sufficient on the App Connector host, transactions can fail due to file descriptor exhaustion; the page's fix is to increase the SYSTEM_FD limit with sudo sysctl -w fs.file-max=1000000.

quotes: If the number of file descriptors is not sufficient on the App Connector host, transactions can fail due to file descriptor exhaustion.
To address this, increase the SYSTEM_FD limit by executing the following command:
sudo sysctl -w fs.file-max=1000000

port-and-fd-metrics.title: Which console or LSS metric reports source-port or file-descriptor use
port-and-fd-metrics.detail: The page names only the notification events and host commands for source ports and file descriptors, and puts the CPU steal figure in the host's status log, not in an LSS field.

current-target-count-field.title: Whether current_target_count is a field of the App Connector status log
current-target-count-field.detail: The monitoring page says the count is stored in a current_target_count field of the App Connector status logs. The App Connector Status log field page and the generated status-log field list contain no field whose name has target in it, while the App Connector Metrics log field table lists TargetCount as the number of targets configured for access via this App Connector. Which log carries the count, and under what name, is not settled by those sources.

disk-floor-vs-event.title: How the 100 MB restart floor relates to the Disk Space Exceeded Limit event
disk-floor-vs-event.detail: The page gives a 100 MB restart floor; the Disk Space Exceeded Limit event takes a threshold of 0 to 2,048 MB with a default of 2,048 (zpa.troubleshooting.events). The relation between the two is not stated.
